subject: Pathology
summary: Cavernous hemangioma is a benign vascular tumour of large, dilated blood‑filled channels that infiltrates surrounding tissue and rarely regresses. It is most common in the liver and can be associated with Von Hippel‑Lindau disease. Imaging and histology guide diagnosis, but percutaneous biopsy is avoided due to bleeding risk.

sections.p: Cavernous hemangioma consists of large, dilated vascular channels separated by connective tissue stroma. It is unencapsulated, infiltrative, and does not regress spontaneously.
b: Benign tumour; most common liver tumour; can be incidental

t.b: Detects hyperechoic lesion with possible central vascularity; suggests benign vascular tumour
Shows hyperintense lesion with peripheral nodular enhancement; classic for cavernous hemangioma
Perilesional enhancement; helps rule out malignancy
Large cavernous spaces with thrombi, calcification, haemosiderin; no capsule

sections.p: No formal staging; lesions are classified by size and symptomatology. Small, asymptomatic lesions are observed; large or symptomatic lesions may require intervention.
b: Size >5 cm or symptomatic = high risk of rupture

sections.p: Idiopathic in most cases; genetic association with Von Hippel‑Lindau disease is the most common inherited cause.
b: Von Hippel‑Lindau disease (cerebellar, retinal, pancreatic, hepatic lesions)

sections.p: Often asymptomatic and found incidentally. Symptomatic lesions may cause pain, fullness, or rupture leading to haemorrhage.
Imaging is the cornerstone; biopsy is contraindicated due to bleeding risk.

t.b: Normal liver echotexture with a well‑defined hyperechoic area suggests haemangioma
Hyperintense signal with peripheral nodular enhancement is diagnostic
Peripheral enhancement with progressive fill‑in supports diagnosis

sections.p: Rupture, haemorrhage, and malignant transformation are rare but serious.
b: Associated with Von Hippel‑Lindau = monitor for other tumours

sections.p: Observation for asymptomatic lesions; intervention for symptomatic or large lesions. Avoid percutaneous biopsy.
b: Avoid biopsy to prevent massive haemorrhage

sections.p: Regular imaging for lesions >5 cm or in Von Hippel‑Lindau patients. No preventive measures for sporadic lesions.
b: Screening for other VHL lesions in affected families

sections.p: Malignant hepatic tumours, focal nodular hyperplasia, and hepatic adenoma.
Small lesions may be missed on ultrasound; biopsy can cause fatal bleeding.
b: Percutaneous biopsy can trigger massive haemorrhage

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with signs of haemodynamic instability

faq.a: No, it is a benign tumour, but it can mimic malignancy on imaging.
The lesion is highly vascular; biopsy can cause life‑threatening bleeding.
Only if the lesion is symptomatic, large, or rapidly growing; many are observed.
